summary: Specifies the cryptographic algorithms and attributes that TCP-AO can use with its manual keying mechanism, and defines how new message authentication codes can be added. Both ends must use the same algorithms to interoperate. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
TCP-AO is a TCP option that lets two computers check that the data between them has not been changed by anyone else. This RFC says which cryptographic algorithms to use for that check and how to turn a shared secret into the per-connection key each check needs.

Two algorithms are required for each job, so that a network can move from the widely deployed SHA-1 option to the stronger AES option without changing the protocol.

subtitle: The cryptographic algorithms that the TCP Authentication Option uses to protect each segment.

tldr.problem: The TCP Authentication Option needs a way to turn a shared secret into a per-connection key, and a way to check that each segment was not altered on the way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC names two key derivation functions, KDF_HMAC_SHA1 and KDF_AES_128_CMAC, and two message authentication codes, HMAC-SHA-1-96 and AES-128-CMAC-96. Each code is paired with the key derivation function that makes its key.
tldr.outcome: All four must be implemented for full compliance, which leaves operators free to move to AES later without a protocol change. The document is a Proposed Standard and the companion to RFC 5925.

today: RFC 5926 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It is the companion to RFC 5925, which defines the TCP Authentication Option, and it names the algorithms and key derivation functions that option uses. The registry it created holds the two algorithm names SHA1 and AES128.

sections.title: What TCP-AO Needs from Cryptography
sections.content:
This document is a companion to RFC 5925, which defines the TCP Authentication Option. Like most modern security protocols, TCP-AO lets the people who run it choose which cryptographic algorithm they want to use to meet their security needs.

TCP-AO provides cryptographic authentication and message integrity verification between two end points. To do that it uses message authentication codes, which rely on shared keys. There are various ways to build such a code. Hash-based codes, the HMACs, are defined in RFC 2104. Cipher-based codes, the CMACs, are defined in NIST SP 800-38B.

This RFC defines the general requirements for the codes used in TCP-AO, both for the ones specified now and for any specified later. It specifies two code algorithms that every TCP-AO implementation must have, and two key derivation functions used to create the traffic keys the codes use. Those two functions are also required of every implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP-AO is a TCP option that lets two computers check that the data between them has not been changed by anyone else. This RFC says which cryptographic algorithms to use for that check and how to turn a shared secret into the per-connection key each check needs.

sections.title: The Required Algorithms
sections.content:
This is the first specification of the cryptography TCP-AO requires. It names two message authentication codes and two key derivation functions, and all four components MUST be implemented for an implementation to be fully compliant.

The required codes are HMAC-SHA-1-96, from RFC 2104 and FIPS 180-3, and AES-128-CMAC-96, from NIST SP 800-38B and FIPS 197. The required key derivation functions are KDF_HMAC_SHA1 and KDF_AES_128_CMAC.

The document also asks for room to change. TCP-AO is meant to support cryptographic agility, so it recommends things for future codes and key derivation functions in several places. For a future code in particular, it SHOULD protect at least 2^48 messages with a collision probability of less than one in 10^9.
sections.plainLanguage: Every implementation has to have two ways of checking the data and two ways of making the per-connection key. The RFC explains later why two of each were asked for.

sections.title: Key Derivation Functions
sections.content:
TCP-AO uses two classes of cryptographic algorithm. Key derivation functions name a pseudorandom function and use a Master_Key and some connection-specific input with that function to produce the Traffic_Keys, the keys used to authenticate and integrity check the individual TCP segments. Message authentication code algorithms take a key and a message and produce an authentication tag used to verify the integrity and authenticity of those messages.

In TCP-AO these algorithms are always used in pairs. Each code algorithm MUST specify the key derivation function to be used with it, though a function MAY be used with more than one code algorithm.

The functions used by the current manual keying of TCP-AO have a fixed interface: Traffic_Key = KDF_alg(Master_Key, Context, Output_Length).

  • KDF_alg is the specific pseudorandom function that is the building block of the derived key.
  • Master_Key is the key shared by both peers in TCP-AO's manual key mode, entered through some interface into their configurations. It is the seed for the function. It is assumed to be a human-readable pre-shared key, so its length may vary. Master_Keys SHOULD be random, but might not be, for example if a user chooses a bad one. For interoperability, the management interface that configures the pre-shared key MUST accept ASCII strings and SHOULD also allow any arbitrary binary string in hexadecimal form. Other configuration methods MAY be supported.
  • Context is a binary string holding information about the specific connection that the derived keying material belongs to, as defined in Section 5.2 of RFC 5925.
  • Output_Length is the length in bits of the key the function will produce, which must be the size the code algorithm needs for its seed.

When it runs, the function generates a string of Output_Length bits from the Master_Key and the context. That string can then be used as a key for any algorithm that takes a key of that length, and a function MAY specify a maximum Output_Length.

The two concrete functions are KDF_HMAC_SHA1, based on the HMAC-SHA1 pseudorandom function, and KDF_AES_128_CMAC, based on the AES-CMAC-PRF-128 function. Both are based on the iteration-mode functions of NIST SP 800-108, which use an underlying pseudorandom function with a fixed-length output, 128 bits for the AES-CMAC and 160 bits for HMAC-SHA1. The output of any length is produced by running the function in a counter mode, where each call uses a different input block distinguished by a block counter.

Each input block is built as (i || Label || Context || Output_Length), where || means concatenation. The counter i is a single octet and always starts at 1. The Label is a binary string that clearly identifies the purpose of the derived keying material; for TCP-AO the ASCII string "TCP-AO" is used, with a capital letter O. The RFC says this label looks like overkill in this specification, since TCP-AO describes only one call to the function, but it is there to comply with FIPS 140 certifications.

The output of several calls is simply concatenated, and truncated to the wanted length. With KDF_HMAC_SHA1, whose internal function produces 160 bits, generating 320 bits means running the function twice, once with i = 1 and once with i = 2, and concatenating the results.
sections.plainLanguage: The per-connection key is computed from the shared secret, the connection details and the length wanted. The computation runs a one-way function several times with a counter, so that different connections get different keys even from the same secret.

sections.title: KDF_AES_128_CMAC and Keys of Any Length
sections.content:
The Master_Key of TCP-AO's manual keying is a shared secret entered by an administrator and passed between two devices out of band, often between two organizations. It does not have to be 16 octets and its length may vary. AES-128-CMAC, however, needs a key of exactly 16 octets, 128 bits, long.

The RFC does not want to force administrators to enter a 16-byte key, so it uses the mechanism of Section 3 of RFC 4615. First, AES-128-CMAC with a fixed key of all zeros is used as a randomness extractor, with the shared secret as the message input, to produce a 128-bit Derived_Master_Key, K. Second, that result is used as the key and AES-128-CMAC is run again, this time with the true input block as the input, to yield the Traffic_Key, TK, used in the code over the message.

The steps are: if the Master_Key is exactly 128 bits, use it as is; otherwise derive K by applying AES-CMAC with the 128-bit all-zero string as the key and the Master_Key as the input message. Then apply AES-CMAC again, with K as the key and the input block as the message. The result is the Traffic_Key, 128 bits long, which is what the code function uses on each TCP segment of the connection.

The RFC RECOMMENDS that deployers use a randomly generated 128-bit string as the Master_Key, but acknowledges that deployers may not. It says it is trying to put a fence around foolishness, as much as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The AES-based option needs a key of exactly 16 bytes, but the shared secret an administrator types can be any length. The RFC turns a secret of any length into a 16-byte key by running it through the cipher-based code with a fixed all-zero key first.

sections.title: The Message Authentication Codes
sections.content:
Each code algorithm defined for TCP-AO has three fixed elements in its definition. KDF_Alg is the name of the key derivation function used to generate the Traffic_Key. Key_Length is the length in bits required for that Traffic_Key. MAC_Length is the final length of the bits used in the TCP-AO MAC field, which may be a truncation of the output the code function normally produces.

The interface is MAC = MAC_alg(Traffic_Key, Message), where Message is the message to be authenticated as specified in Section 5.1 of RFC 5925.

Two code options are specified. HMAC-SHA-1-96 is based on RFC 2104 and FIPS 180-3, and AES-128-CMAC-96 is based on NIST SP 800-38B and FIPS 197. Both give a high level of security and efficiency. AES-128-CMAC-96 is potentially more efficient, particularly in hardware, but HMAC-SHA-1-96 is more widely used in Internet protocols and in most cases could be supported with little or no additional code in today's deployed software and devices.

One detail matters for the design: the outputs are truncated to 96 bits. AES-128-CMAC produces a 128-bit code and HMAC-SHA-1 produces a 160-bit result, and the output is then cut down to 96 bits as a trade-off between security and message size, so that it fits in the TCP-AO option field.

For HMAC-SHA-1-96 the three elements are KDF_HMAC_SHA1, a key length of 160 bits and a code length of 96 bits. For AES-128-CMAC-96 they are KDF_AES_128_CMAC, a key length of 128 bits and a code length of 96 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The code that checks the data comes in two forms, one built on SHA-1 and one built on AES. Both produce a fixed-size tag of 96 bits, cut down from their natural output so that it fits in the TCP option.

sections.title: What a Configuration Screen Should Show
sections.content:
The RFC gives suggested names for the two key derivation functions so that different products can be set up the same way. A user interface SHOULD refer to KDF_HMAC_SHA1 simply as "SHA1" and KDF_AES_128_CMAC simply as "AES128". The initial values in the IANA registry match those two entries.

A user interface SHOULD use KDF_HMAC_SHA1 as the default selection in TCP-AO settings. KDF_HMAC_SHA1 is preferred at this time because it has wide support, being present in most of the implementations in the marketplace.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC asks for the two options to be called SHA1 and AES128 in configuration menus, so that a network engineer sees the same names on every product, and it asks for SHA1 to be the default because most products already have it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document inherits all the security considerations of TCP-AO in RFC 5925, of AES-CMAC in RFC 4493 and of HMAC-SHA-1 in RFC 2104.

The security of a system built on cryptography depends on the strength of the algorithms chosen and on the strength of the keys used with them. It also depends on the engineering of the protocol, so that there is no non-cryptographic way to get around the protection.

Care should be taken that the selected key is unpredictable and avoids any key known to be weak for the algorithm in use. RFC 4086 has helpful information on key generation and on cryptographic randomness.

The RFC notes that in KDF_AES_128_CMAC the function needs a 128-bit key as its seed, and that it did not want to force administrators to enter a 16-byte Master_Key, so a sub-key routine was specified that handles a variable length one. That does not make it safe for administrators to use weak keys, and it is encouraged to follow RFC 4086. The RFC says it simply tried to put a fence around foolishness, as much as possible.

The algorithms marked as MUST implement are not known to be broken at the time of writing, and the RFC expects new revisions of the document as time goes by, so implementers should look for a more recent version.

Why two code algorithms were mandated: SHA-1 was selected because it is widely deployed and has sufficient strength and reasonable computational cost, so it is a MUST for TCP-AO today. The security strength of SHA-1 HMACs should be enough for the foreseeable future, especially as the tags are truncated to 96 bits. Recently exposed vulnerabilities in other codes, such as MD5, are not practical against HMAC-SHA-1, though such analyses are mounting and could one day matter. The security issues driving the move from SHA-1 to SHA-256 for digital signatures do not immediately make SHA-1 weak in HMAC mode. AES-128 CMAC is considered stronger than SHA-1 but may not yet have very wide implementation, and it is also a MUST so that vendors move towards it and so there is another option if SHA-1 is compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: The choice of algorithm is only half of it. A strong algorithm with a weak key is still weak, so the RFC keeps pointing at the guidance on generating random keys, and it explains why it asked for two algorithms rather than one.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has created a registry named "Cryptographic Algorithms for TCP-AO Registration", with the procedure RFC Publication after Expert Review. Its initial contents are two entries: SHA1 and AES128, both with this RFC as their reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The two algorithms were given registry names, SHA1 and AES128, so that products can name them the same way.
